steps.ask: Which part of the margin of error formula changes when $n$ changes, and which part stays the same?
steps.title: Write the margin of error using n

lines.text: Let $k = 1.96\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}$. It does not change, so the margin of error is $\frac{k}{\sqrt{n}}$.

problems.note: Changes from calculating n to judging four statements about how the standard error responds to the sample size and p-hat. No numbers are calculated, so the method is different; it is the only other candidate for this skill.

steps.ask: A higher confidence level changes which $z$-value is used. What does a bigger $z$-value do to the margin of error?
steps.title: Statement 1: Always true

lines.text: A higher confidence level needs a larger $z$-value, so the margin of error, and the interval, gets wider.

steps.ask: Does $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ always go up or always go down as $\hat{p}$ changes? Try $\hat{p} = 0$, $0.5$ and $1$.
steps.title: Statement 2: Sometimes true

lines.text: $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ increases as $\hat{p}$ rises towards $0.5$ and then decreases, so the standard error does not always increase.

steps.ask: With $n$ fixed, what happens to the standard error when $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ rises?
steps.title: Statement 3: Always true

lines.text: With $\hl{1}{n}$ fixed, the standard error is the square root of $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ divided by $\hl{1}{n}$, so it rises whenever $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ rises.

steps.ask: What happens to a fraction when its denominator gets bigger?
steps.title: Statement 4: Never true

lines.text: Increasing $\hl{1}{n}$ makes $\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{\hl{1}{n}}$ smaller, so the standard error always decreases.

steps.ask: What does the letter $p$ stand for in this question? Say it in words.

lines.text: $p$ is the proportion of all the café's customers who order a vegan meal.

steps.ask: What does the null hypothesis say about $p$, and how do you write 30% as a decimal?
steps.title: Write the hypotheses

lines.text: $H_0$ says the claim is true.
$H_1$ says the claim is false: $p \ne \hl{1}{0.3}$.

steps.ask: Where does the claimed value sit relative to the confidence interval, and what does that mean for $H_0$?
steps.title: Possible conclusions

lines.text: If $\hl{1}{0.3}$ is inside the confidence interval, do not reject $H_0$: the sample supports the claim. If it is outside, reject $H_0$: there is evidence that the claim is wrong.

problems.note: Changes from writing the hypotheses to also building a confidence interval from a sample and deciding. The parameter is still a proportion, and the claimed value is now 20%.

lines.text: $H_0$: $p = \hl{1}{20\%}$ (the claim is true).
$H_1$: $p \ne \hl{1}{20\%}$ (the claim is false).

lines.text: $\hl{1}{20\%}$ is outside the interval, so reject $H_0$. There is evidence that more than $\hl{1}{20\%}$ of students cycle.

problems.note: Changes to a z-test on a mean with a standard deviation, so the method is different. The final step still states what the result means in context.

steps.ask: Which numbers go into $\bar{x}$, $\mu$, $s$ and $n$ in this formula?
steps.title: Find the test statistic

lines.text: Use $z = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}}$.

steps.ask: What are the two-tailed critical values at the 5% level, and how does $z$ compare with them?
steps.title: Compare with the critical values

lines.text: At the 5% level, two-tailed, the critical values are $\pm 1.96$.

steps.ask: Is $z$ inside or outside $[-1.96,\ 1.96]$, and what does that say about the 50-minute claim?
steps.title: Conclude in context

lines.text: $\hl{1}{z}$ is outside $[-1.96,\ 1.96]$, so reject $H_0$. There is evidence that the mean homework time is not $\hl{2}{50}$ minutes. It is probably longer.

steps.ask: What is the difference between the two sample means, and why could it happen?
steps.title: Compare the two samples

lines.text: The samples give different means because different students were chosen. This is sampling variability.

steps.ask: Is either sample mean exactly the mean for the whole school, and what does that mean for trusting one sample?
steps.title: Be cautious

lines.text: Neither sample mean is exactly the school mean, so we should not rely on one sample alone.

steps.ask: The two samples are the same size. How should the two means be combined?
steps.title: Combine the samples

lines.text: The samples are the same size, so average the two means.
